items.prompt: `once(fn)` tracks a separate `called` boolean instead of testing `if (result !== undefined) return result`. Which wrapped function would break the shortcut version?
items.answer: One that really returns undefined, like an init routine, since it would rerun on every call
distractors: One that throws on its first call, because the shortcut version would cache the thrown error forever
One that returns a promise, because a pending promise compares equal to undefined until it settles
One that takes arguments, because the shortcut version caches the result per argument list
items.explanation: closures/solution.js: `called` records that fn ran at all, independent of what it returned; `result` alone cannot tell 'never ran' from 'ran and returned undefined'.

items.prompt: memoize's default cache key is `JSON.stringify(args)`. What is the trade-off of that key choice?
items.answer: Equal-looking but different objects share one entry, and values JSON drops or mangles can collide
distractors: Every call with an object argument misses the cache, because objects are compared by reference
The cache stays at a single entry, because each new key string replaces the previous one
Primitive arguments are skipped, because JSON.stringify serializes just objects and arrays
items.explanation: The key is a string of the arguments' JSON: structurally equal arguments map to the same Map key, and anything JSON cannot represent faithfully (functions, undefined, Dates) may collapse; pass a keyFn when identity matters.

items.prompt: `createRateLimiter(2, 1000, nowFn)` is called at t = 0, 500, 900 and 1000 ms. What do the four calls return?
items.answer: true, true, false, true: the refused 900 call is not stored, and by 1000 the t=0 stamp aged out
distractors: true, true, false, false: the window resets only once the most recent stamp is older than 1000 ms
true, true, true, false: each call drops the oldest stamp before it checks against the limit
true, false, false, true: the limiter allows one call per 500 ms slice of the 1000 ms window
items.explanation: Stamps with `now - timestamps[0] >= windowMs` are shifted out first; a call is refused when two stamps remain, and refused calls never push a stamp.

items.prompt: withTimeout races the work against a timer promise and ends with `.finally(() => clearTimeout(timer))`. What goes wrong if that finally is removed and the work wins the race?
items.answer: The timer still fires later, keeping a Node process alive until then for a wasted rejection
distractors: The result is replaced by the Timeout error, because a later rejection overrides an earlier resolve
The work promise is cancelled, because Promise.race aborts whichever entry finishes second
An unhandled-rejection crash occurs, because nobody is listening to the timer promise any more
items.explanation: Promise.race settles once, so a late rejection is ignored (race still handles it), but the pending setTimeout keeps the event loop busy until it fires; clearing it releases the timer.

items.prompt: In concurrencyLimit, each worker stores `results[currentIndex] = await ...` rather than `results.push(await ...)`. What would push get wrong?
items.answer: Results would land in completion order, so a slow first task would not end up at index 0
distractors: push would make the workers run one at a time, because push waits for a lock on the array
push would drop results of tasks that throw, while index assignment records them as undefined
push would double-count tasks, because two workers can push the same task's result
items.explanation: The drill promises 'results in original task order, with only 2 running at once'; writing by the claimed index keeps input order while tasks finish in any order.

items.prompt: Each worker copies `nextIndex` into `currentIndex` and increments it before awaiting the task. Why must the claim happen before the await?
items.answer: Other workers run while this one waits at the await, so claiming first stops two starting one task
distractors: Incrementing after the await would throw, because the loop condition is checked only once per worker
The await would otherwise capture a stale copy of nextIndex, and the worker would never advance
JavaScript runs workers on separate threads, so the increment has to happen before the lock is released
items.explanation: Single-threaded but interleaved: between await points other workers' loops run; the synchronous claim (read + increment) has no await in between.

items.prompt: debounceAsync returns a promise per call. Why does each new call invoke `rejectPrevious(new Error('Debounced by a newer call'))`?
items.answer: Its timer was cleared, so the earlier promise would never settle and its caller would hang
distractors: Rejecting cancels the network request the earlier call already started inside fn
The earlier promise would otherwise resolve with the newer call's result as well and duplicate it
It frees the timer slot, because setTimeout allows only one pending timer per closure
items.explanation: clearTimeout(timer) means the old callback never runs; its resolve/reject would never be called, so the code rejects it explicitly.

items.prompt: allSettledClone is built on Promise.all, which rejects on the first failure. Why does the clone still never reject?
items.answer: A .then rejection handler turns each failure into a status object, so Promise.all only sees values
distractors: Promise.resolve(promise) swallows rejections, so the failed inputs simply arrive as undefined values
The clone wraps Promise.all in try/catch and returns the partial results when anything fails
Promise.all only rejects for thrown errors, not for promises that were rejected with Error objects
items.explanation: `.then(value => ({status:'fulfilled', value}), reason => ({status:'rejected', reason}))` converts every outcome into a fulfilled value before Promise.all combines them.

items.prompt: createTaskQueue starts tasks with `Promise.resolve().then(item.task)` rather than calling `item.task()` directly. What does that protect against?
items.answer: A synchronous throw becomes a rejection for its caller, and finally still frees the slot
distractors: It makes the tasks run in parallel worker threads instead of on the main event loop
It guarantees tasks finish in the order they were enqueued, regardless of how long each takes
It retries a failing task once before rejecting the promise that enqueue returned
items.explanation: A direct `item.task()` that throws would escape runNext with `active` already incremented, wedging the queue; inside .then the throw becomes a rejection routed to item.reject, and .finally decrements active and calls runNext.

items.prompt: The script logs '1', schedules setTimeout(log '2', 0), schedules Promise.resolve().then(log '3'), then logs '4'. Why does it print 1, 4, 3, 2?
items.answer: Sync code runs first, then the promise callback as a microtask, before the timer's macrotask
distractors: setTimeout 0 is clamped to 4 ms, and the promise callback simply happens to be faster than that
Promise callbacks have higher thread priority, so they interrupt the current script after '1'
Callbacks run in reverse order of scheduling, so the later promise runs before the earlier timer
items.explanation: The call stack must empty first; microtasks (promises) run after the current script but before the next macrotask (setTimeout).

items.prompt: processChunk handles 100 items, then reschedules itself with queueMicrotask. Why can a 10,000-item run still freeze the UI?
items.answer: Microtasks run to completion before rendering, so a self-rescheduling chain never yields to paint
distractors: splice copies the whole remaining array each time, and that copying alone blocks the main thread
queueMicrotask waits for the next animation frame, so the work stretches over many frames
Microtasks run on a background thread whose results are only drawn once every chunk has finished
items.explanation: Microtasks run after the current script but before rendering; yield with setTimeout or requestAnimationFrame (the file's 'or better: rAF') between chunks.

items.prompt: A long-lived SPA registers the handler returned by createLeakyHandler, which reads `bigData.length`. Why is the million-element array never garbage-collected?
items.answer: The handler is reachable and its closure references bigData, so the array stays reachable
distractors: Arrays created with fill() are allocated outside the JS heap and have to be freed manually
The garbage collector skips any object larger than its young-generation size limit
console.log keeps a reference to every value it has printed, for the DevTools console
items.explanation: The GC only collects objects with no strong references from roots; closures and listeners are the usual suspects. Remove the listener or stop referencing the data in the closure.

items.front: `nums.map(x => { x * 2 })` is expected to double [1,2,3], but the result logs as an array of undefined. Why?
items.back: Braces make the arrow a block body, which returns nothing unless it says `return`. Fix: `x => x * 2` (expression body) or `x => { return x * 2; }`.

items.front: A cart total is `items.reduce((acc, n) => acc + n)` with no initial value. It works in every test, then an empty cart is checked out. What happens?
items.back: reduce on an empty array with no initial value throws a TypeError, so the empty case crashes. Fix: always pass the initial value, e.g. `reduce((acc, n) => acc + n, 0)`.

items.front: Code wraps `doAsync().catch(e => {})` in try { } catch (e) { }, and failures of doAsync leave no trace anywhere. What two mistakes are stacked here?
items.back: A sync try/catch cannot catch a promise rejection, and the empty .catch swallows the error silently. Fix: `await` inside try/catch (or a real .catch) that logs and rethrows or handles it.

items.front: Inside an async function, `const p = fetch("/data"); console.log(p);` prints `Promise { <pending> }` instead of the data. What is wrong?
items.back: The await is missing, so p is the promise, not the response. Fix: `const res = await fetch("/data")` (then check res.ok and await res.json()); wrap the await in try/catch to avoid unhandled rejections.
